Section 3.1 — The Call to the Ministry

Before a man asks how to do the work of a pastor, he must settle a prior and more searching question: has God called him to it at all? There are two errors here, and both have wrecked churches. The first is the man who runs without being sent — ambitious, gifted perhaps, but never truly summoned, building a ministry as he would build a business. The second is the man who flees when he has plainly been sent — like Jonah, like Moses at the bush, hiding behind his unworthiness to escape a burden God has laid on him. The doctrine of calling is meant to deliver us from both: from presumption on the one hand and from disobedient cowardice on the other.

Scripture treats the desire for this work as a good thing, but never as a sufficient thing. "If a man desires the position of a bishop, he desires a good work" (1 Timothy 3:1). The desire is honorable; it is the first stirring of a true call. But desire alone ordains no one. A genuine call has two parts that must meet. There is the internal call — that holy compulsion Paul describes when he says, "woe is me if I do not preach the gospel!" (1 Corinthians 9:16). It is not mere willingness; it is a constraint, a sense that one cannot finally be at peace doing anything else. And there is the external call — the confirmation of the church, which examines a man's gifts and his character and recognizes the hand of God upon him. A man does not ordain himself. The inward fire must be confirmed by the outward judgment of God's people, or it is not yet a call but only a feeling.

And once both have met, the man must feel the weight of what he has taken up. He is now responsible for souls for whom Christ shed His blood, and, as we saw in Unit 1, he will be judged as a teacher, by a stricter standard than the rest of the flock. This is not a career. It is a stewardship of eternal things, and it should be entered soberly, with trembling as much as with joy.
Section 3.2 — The Qualifications: Character Before Competence

A word before we go further on how this unit uses "he" and "his" for this office, and on where CTS stands. The requirement that this leader be "the husband of one wife" (1 Timothy 3:2; Titus 1:6) sits at the center of a real disagreement among Bible-believing Christians, so this course lays out three positions rather than treat the question as settled. The complementarian view reads the qualification lists, with 1 Timothy 2:12, as reserving the senior pastoral and eldership office for qualified men, while affirming women's gifting in the church's other ministries. The egalitarian view points to texts such as Galatians 3:28, Philip's four daughters who prophesied (Acts 21:9), and Paul's own regulation of women praying and prophesying in the gathered assembly (1 Corinthians 11:5), arguing a called and qualified woman may hold any ministry office. A third, team-ministry view holds that women may serve in substantial, even titled pastoral roles, while the senior or lead pastor remains a man, so that women's leadership operates under that oversight. This unit describes the qualifications below in the text's own traditional masculine language, without that settling the question for you. Where you land is a matter for your own study, conscience, and the church body you serve.

When the Spirit, through Paul, lists the qualifications for this office, the result should astonish anyone who has spent time in the world's leadership culture. Read 1 Timothy 3:1–7 and Titus 1:5–9 side by side and ask a simple question of each item: is this a skill, or is it a matter of character? You will find that nearly the entire list is character. Above reproach. The husband of one wife. Temperate, sober-minded, of good behavior. Not given to wine, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not greedy for money. One who rules his own house well. Not a new convert. Of good testimony even among those outside the church.

And amid that long catalog of character, how much room is given to raw competency? Very little, and what is given is not about talent or charisma but about the ministry itself: he must be able to teach, and Titus adds that he must hold firmly to sound doctrine so that he can both exhort believers and refute those who contradict it (Titus 1:9). Even household management, listed alongside the character qualities, carries a real leadership dimension — Paul reasons that a man who cannot manage his own household well has not shown he can care for God's household either (1 Timothy 3:4–5). So the list is not pure character with zero competence attached; but character overwhelmingly dominates it, and the competencies required are modest and ministry-shaped rather than the markers the world prizes. The world assembles its leaders by talent — who is the most capable, the most charismatic, the most effective. God assembles His shepherds by holiness first, with sound teaching and demonstrated, humble leadership required alongside it. This is one of the most counter-cultural truths a seminarian will ever absorb, and it must be absorbed deep, because the temptation to reverse it never lets up. A church that selects its leaders the way a corporation selects executives — for giftedness while winking at character — is sowing a harvest of grief it will reap within the decade.

Notice too the warning against ordaining a new convert, "lest being puffed up with pride he fall into the same condemnation as the devil" (1 Timothy 3:6). The danger named there is not incompetence; it is pride. And notice the requirement of a good reputation with outsiders. The man's character must be visible and verified not only inside the warm circle of the church but out in the cold light of the marketplace, where reputations are not flattered. God screens His shepherds by who they are when no one is applauding.
Section 3.3 — Holiness, Humility, and the Spiritual Disciplines

If the office is given to character, then the pastor's first and most neglected labor is the tending of his own soul. Paul's charge to Timothy puts the order beyond dispute: "Take heed to yourself and to the doctrine" (1 Timothy 4:16). To yourself first, and then to the doctrine. The man who reverses that — who pours all his care into his teaching while his own heart goes untended — is building a fine house on a rotting foundation. You cannot give your people water from a cistern you have let run dry. Every public word a pastor speaks should be drawn from a private well he is daily refilling in secret, alone with God.

This is why the spiritual disciplines are not optional refinements for the unusually devout pastor; they are the very supply lines of the ministry. Prayer that is more than the hurried blessing before a meal. The Word read for his own soul and not merely mined for next Sunday's sermon — for a man can study the Scriptures professionally for years and starve spiritually the whole time, handling the bread of life as a baker who never eats. There must be secret communion that no congregation ever sees, a hidden life with God behind the public life of ministry. The visible man in the pulpit must be matched by an invisible man on his knees, or the visible man will eventually become a hollow performance.

And over all of it must hang the guard of humility, for pride is the peculiar and besetting sin of those who handle holy things. The very platform that makes a man useful makes him a target; the higher he is lifted in the eyes of others, the deeper the pit that opens beneath his vanity. The shepherd who forgets that he is first a sheep, equally dependent on the grace he proclaims, has already begun to fall, however long it takes the fall to become visible. Keep low. The ground is safest there.

Consider how Nehemiah went about the great work of his life. When word reached him that the wall of Jerusalem was broken down and its gates burned, he did not first reach for a plan. He broke down and wept. He fasted and prayed, confessing the sin of his fathers and his own, and only then, after months of waiting on God, did he set out to build. And notice what kind of builder he was. He did not ride into the city announcing himself or rush the people into stacking bricks. He arose at night, while everyone slept, and rode quietly around the ruins — over rubble so bad that in places he had to go on foot — until he had seen the worst of it for himself and made an honest survey of the facts. Then he laid his plans. The inner work came before the outer; the honest look came before the bold call. And when the work was underway and his enemies tried every weapon to stop it — they laughed at him, they ridiculed him, they tried blackmail, they schemed to lure him away and kill him — he gave them one answer and kept building: "I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down" (Nehemiah 6:3). He does the hidden work of prayer and self-examination before the public work begins, he tells himself the truth about the ruins before he sounds the trumpet, and once he knows the work is God’s, he refuses to be argued, flattered, or frightened down off the wall.
Section 3.4 — The Pastor as Example, and Guarding Against Disqualification

We return now to a truth first sounded in Unit 1, because it is the hinge of pastoral character: the pastor leads chiefly by what he is. Peter charges the elders to shepherd the flock "being examples to the flock" (1 Peter 5:3). The people will become, over time, more like what they watch their shepherd be than like what they hear him say. This is a glorious privilege and a terrifying responsibility in the same breath.

And because the stakes are so high, every pastor must reckon honestly with the possibility of his own ruin. Here is a truth I want pressed into you: moral catastrophe is almost never a sudden leap. It is a slow drift — a series of small, deniable compromises, each one excused, that quietly carve a channel down which the final disaster will one day rush. The unguarded glance becomes the entertained thought; the entertained thought becomes the secret habit; the secret habit becomes the public scandal that ends a ministry. No man wakes up one morning and decides to destroy his life's work. He drifts there, one unconfessed inch at a time. Even the apostle Paul refused to presume on his own standing: "I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, lest, when I have preached to others, I myself should become disqualified" (1 Corinthians 9:27). If Paul guarded himself, the man who thinks he has no need to is the man already in gravest danger.

What, then, are the safeguards? Honest accountability to men who are permitted to ask the hard questions and will not be flattered out of asking them. A vigilant guard over the eyes, the schedule, and the private hours, where ruin is always seeded. A refusal to minister from isolation, for the lone shepherd, cut off and accountable to no one, is the easiest of all to pick off. And the immediate confession of sin while it is still small, before it has had time to take root and grow strong in the dark. A pastor must also guard his marriage as part of guarding his ministry — a matter so weighty that we devote the next unit to it. The whole aim of this vigilance is summed up in the testimony every faithful minister longs to give at the end: "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith" (2 Timothy 4:7). The goal is not merely to begin well. It is to finish.

mc.stem: 1. The two errors concerning the call to ministry are running without being sent and:
mc.why: The doctrine of calling delivers from both presumption (running unsent) and disobedient cowardice (fleeing when sent).

es_reference.stem: 1. Los dos errores acerca del llamamiento al ministerio son correr sin ser enviado y:
options: huir cuando claramente se es enviado
es_reference.why: La doctrina del llamamiento libra de ambos: de la presunción (correr sin ser enviado) y de la cobardía desobediente (huir cuando se es enviado).

mc.stem: 2. 1 Timothy 3:1 treats the desire for the office as:
options: a good thing, but not a sufficient thing
proof of a genuine call by itself
mc.why: The desire is honorable—the first stirring of a true call—but desire alone ordains no one.

es_reference.stem: 2. 1 Timoteo 3:1 trata el deseo del oficio como:
options: algo bueno, pero no algo suficiente
prueba de un llamamiento genuino por sí solo
es_reference.why: El deseo es honroso — el primer despertar de un llamamiento verdadero — pero el deseo solo no ordena a nadie.

mc.stem: 3. The “internal call” is illustrated by Paul's words:
options: “woe is me if I do not preach the gospel”
mc.why: The internal call is the holy constraint Paul names: ‘woe is me if I do not preach the gospel.’

es_reference.stem: 3. El «llamamiento interno» se ilustra con las palabras de Pablo:
options: «¡ay de mí si no anunciare el evangelio!»
es_reference.why: El llamamiento interno es la santa restricción que Pablo nombra: «¡ay de mí si no anunciare el evangelio!»

mc.stem: 4. The “external call” consists of:
options: the church confirming a man's gifts and character
mc.why: The inward fire must be confirmed by the church's examination of a man's gifts and character, or it is only a feeling.

es_reference.stem: 4. El «llamamiento externo» consiste en:
options: la iglesia confirmando los dones y el carácter de un hombre
es_reference.why: El fuego interior debe ser confirmado por el examen que la iglesia hace de los dones y el carácter, o es solo un sentimiento.

mc.stem: 5. The unit insists that a man does not:
options: feel the weight of the office
mc.why: A man does not ordain himself; the internal call must meet the external confirmation of God's people.

es_reference.stem: 5. La unidad insiste en que un hombre no:
es_reference.why: Un hombre no se ordena a sí mismo; el llamamiento interno debe encontrarse con la confirmación externa del pueblo de Dios.

mc.stem: 6. Reading 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1, nearly all the qualifications concern:
mc.why: Asked of each item whether it is a skill or character, nearly the entire list is character.

es_reference.stem: 6. Al leer 1 Timoteo 3 y Tito 1, casi todos los requisitos tienen que ver con:
es_reference.why: Preguntando de cada punto si es destreza o carácter, casi toda la lista es carácter.

mc.stem: 7. The one practical competency essentially required of an elder is that he be:
mc.why: Amid a long catalog of character, the specific teaching skill named is that he be able to teach — though Titus adds exhorting and refuting error, and household management carries its own leadership dimension.

es_reference.stem: 7. La única competencia práctica esencialmente requerida de un anciano es que sea:
es_reference.why: En medio de un largo catálogo de carácter, la destreza específica de enseñanza mencionada es que sea apto para enseñar — aunque Tito añade exhortar y refutar el error, y el gobierno del hogar lleva su propia dimensión de liderazgo.

mc.stem: 8. The world assembles leaders by talent; God assembles His shepherds by:
mc.why: The world gathers leaders by talent; God assembles shepherds by holiness, with one competency added.

es_reference.stem: 8. El mundo reúne a sus líderes por el talento; Dios reúne a sus pastores por:
es_reference.why: El mundo reúne líderes por el talento; Dios reúne pastores por la santidad, con una sola competencia añadida.

mc.stem: 9. The warning against ordaining a new convert (1 Timothy 3:6) names which danger?
mc.why: The danger named is not incompetence but pride—being puffed up and falling into the condemnation of the devil.

es_reference.stem: 9. La advertencia contra ordenar a un nuevo convertido (1 Timoteo 3:6) nombra ¿cuál peligro?
es_reference.why: El peligro nombrado no es la incompetencia sino el orgullo — envanecerse y caer en la condenación del diablo.

mc.stem: 10. A church selecting leaders the way a corporation selects executives is:
mc.why: Choosing for giftedness while winking at character sows a harvest of grief it will reap within the decade.

es_reference.stem: 10. Una iglesia que selecciona líderes como una corporación selecciona ejecutivos está:
es_reference.why: Escoger por la aptitud mientras se guiña el ojo al carácter siembra una cosecha de dolor que segará dentro de la década.

mc.stem: 11. “Take heed to yourself and to the doctrine” establishes that the pastor must attend first to:
mc.why: To yourself first, then the doctrine; the man who reverses it builds a fine house on a rotting foundation.

es_reference.stem: 11. «Ten cuidado de ti mismo y de la doctrina» establece que el pastor debe atender primero a:
es_reference.why: A ti mismo primero, luego la doctrina; el que lo invierte edifica una hermosa casa sobre un cimiento podrido.

mc.stem: 12. The image of a dry cistern teaches that a pastor cannot:
options: give his people water he has let run dry
mc.why: You cannot give your people water from a cistern you have let run dry; the private well must be daily refilled.

es_reference.stem: 12. La imagen de una cisterna seca enseña que un pastor no puede:
options: dar a su gente agua que ha dejado secar
es_reference.why: Usted no puede dar a su gente agua de una cisterna que ha dejado secar; el pozo privado debe llenarse a diario.

mc.stem: 13. The spiritual disciplines are described as:
options: the supply lines of the ministry
mc.why: They are not optional refinements but the very supply lines of the ministry.

es_reference.stem: 13. Las disciplinas espirituales se describen como:
options: las líneas de abastecimiento del ministerio
es_reference.why: No son refinamientos opcionales sino las líneas mismas de abastecimiento del ministerio.

mc.stem: 14. The unit calls which the “peculiar and besetting” sin of those who handle holy things?
mc.why: Pride is the peculiar and besetting sin of those who handle holy things; the platform that makes a man useful makes him a target.

es_reference.stem: 14. ¿A cuál llama la unidad el pecado «peculiar y acosador» de quienes manejan cosas santas?
es_reference.why: El orgullo es el pecado peculiar y acosador de quienes manejan cosas santas; la plataforma que hace útil a un hombre lo hace blanco.

mc.stem: 15. The shepherd who forgets that he is first a sheep has:
mc.why: The shepherd who forgets he is first a sheep, equally dependent on grace, has already begun to fall.

es_reference.stem: 15. El pastor que olvida que es primero una oveja ha:
es_reference.why: El pastor que olvida que es primero una oveja, igualmente dependiente de la gracia, ya ha comenzado a caer.

mc.stem: 16. The pastor leads the flock chiefly by:
mc.why: The people become, over time, more like what they watch their shepherd be than what they hear him say.

es_reference.stem: 16. El pastor dirige la grey principalmente por:
es_reference.why: Con el tiempo, la gente llega a ser más parecida a lo que ve que su pastor es que a lo que le oye decir.

mc.stem: 17. Moral catastrophe in ministry is almost never:
mc.why: It is a slow drift—small, deniable compromises—not a sudden leap; no man wakes up and decides to destroy his life's work.

es_reference.stem: 17. La catástrofe moral en el ministerio casi nunca es:
es_reference.why: Es una deriva lenta — concesiones pequeñas y negables — no un salto repentino; nadie despierta y decide destruir la obra de su vida.

mc.stem: 18. The progression of moral drift runs from the unguarded glance to the entertained thought to:
mc.why: The unguarded glance becomes the entertained thought; the thought becomes the secret habit; the habit becomes the public scandal.

es_reference.stem: 18. La progresión de la deriva moral va de la mirada sin guardia al pensamiento entretenido y luego a:
es_reference.why: La mirada sin guardia se vuelve el pensamiento entretenido; el pensamiento, el hábito secreto; el hábito, el escándalo público.

mc.stem: 19. That even Paul disciplined himself (1 Corinthians 9:27) teaches that the man in gravest danger is the one who:
options: thinks he has no need to guard himself
mc.why: If Paul guarded himself lest he be disqualified, the man who thinks he need not is already in gravest danger.

es_reference.stem: 19. Que aun Pablo se disciplinara (1 Corintios 9:27) enseña que el hombre en más grave peligro es el que:
options: cree no tener necesidad de guardarse
es_reference.why: Si Pablo se guardaba para no ser reprobado, el que cree no tener necesidad ya está en el más grave peligro.

mc.stem: 20. The whole aim of pastoral vigilance is summed up in Paul's testimony that he had:
options: finished the race and kept the faith
mc.why: The goal is not merely to begin well but to finish: ‘I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.’

es_reference.stem: 20. Todo el propósito de la vigilancia pastoral se resume en el testimonio de Pablo de que había:
options: acabado la carrera y guardado la fe
es_reference.why: La meta no es meramente comenzar bien sino terminar: «He peleado la buena batalla, he acabado la carrera, he guardado la fe».

sa.prompt: 21. Name the two errors regarding the call to ministry and how the doctrine of calling delivers from both.
sa.model: The first error is the man who runs without being sent—gifted perhaps, but never truly summoned, building a ministry as he would a business. The second is the man who flees when he has plainly been sent, like Jonah or Moses at the bush, hiding behind his unworthiness to escape a burden God has laid on him. The doctrine of calling is meant to deliver from both: from presumption on the one hand and from disobedient cowardice on the other.

es_reference.prompt: 21. Nombre los dos errores respecto al llamamiento al ministerio y cómo la doctrina del llamamiento libra de ambos.
es_reference.model: El primer error es el hombre que corre sin ser enviado — dotado quizá, pero nunca verdaderamente convocado, edificando un ministerio como edificaría un negocio. El segundo es el hombre que huye cuando claramente ha sido enviado, como Jonás o Moisés en la zarza, escondiéndose tras su indignidad para escapar de una carga que Dios le ha puesto. La doctrina del llamamiento busca librar de ambos: de la presunción por un lado y de la cobardía desobediente por el otro.

sa.prompt: 22. Distinguish the internal and external call, and why both must meet.
sa.model: A genuine call has two parts that must meet. The internal call is the holy compulsion Paul describes—‘woe is me if I do not preach the gospel’—not mere willingness but a constraint, a sense that one cannot finally be at peace doing anything else. The external call is the confirmation of the church, which examines a man's gifts and character and recognizes God's hand on him. A man does not ordain himself; the inward fire must be confirmed by the outward judgment of God's people, or it is not yet a call but only a feeling.

es_reference.prompt: 22. Distinga el llamamiento interno y el externo, y por qué ambos deben encontrarse.
es_reference.model: Un llamamiento genuino tiene dos partes que deben encontrarse. El llamamiento interno es la santa compulsión que Pablo describe — «¡ay de mí si no anunciare el evangelio!» — no mera disposición sino una restricción, un sentir de que uno no puede finalmente estar en paz haciendo cualquier otra cosa. El llamamiento externo es la confirmación de la iglesia, que examina los dones y el carácter de un hombre y reconoce la mano de Dios sobre él. Un hombre no se ordena a sí mismo; el fuego interior debe ser confirmado por el juicio exterior del pueblo de Dios, o todavía no es un llamamiento sino solo un sentimiento.

sa.prompt: 23. Why are the qualifications for the office almost entirely about character rather than skill?
sa.model: Reading 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1 and asking of each item whether it is a skill or a matter of character, one finds nearly the entire list is character: above reproach, temperate, gentle, not greedy, ruling his own house well. What competence is required is modest and ministry-shaped: he must be able to teach, and Titus adds holding firmly to sound doctrine so he can exhort and refute error, while household management itself carries a real leadership dimension. The world assembles leaders by talent—the most capable and charismatic—but God assembles His shepherds by holiness first, with sound teaching and demonstrated leadership required alongside it. This is among the most counter-cultural truths a seminarian will absorb, and the temptation to reverse it never lets up.

es_reference.prompt: 23. ¿Por qué los requisitos del oficio son casi enteramente de carácter y no de destreza?
es_reference.model: Al leer 1 Timoteo 3 y Tito 1 y preguntar de cada punto si es destreza o asunto de carácter, se halla que casi toda la lista es carácter: irreprensible, sobrio, amable, no avaro, que gobierna bien su propia casa. Lo que se requiere en competencia es modesto y moldeado por el ministerio: debe ser apto para enseñar, y Tito añade sostener firmemente la sana doctrina para poder exhortar y refutar el error, mientras que el gobierno del hogar mismo lleva una verdadera dimensión de liderazgo. El mundo reúne líderes por el talento — los más capaces y carismáticos — pero Dios reúne a sus pastores por la santidad primero, con sana enseñanza y liderazgo demostrado requeridos junto a ella. Esta es de las verdades más contraculturales que un seminarista absorberá, y la tentación de invertirla nunca cede.

sa.prompt: 24. Why does the unit warn against ordaining a new convert and require a good reputation with outsiders?
sa.model: The warning against ordaining a new convert (1 Timothy 3:6) names not incompetence but pride—lest, being puffed up, he fall into the same condemnation as the devil. The requirement of a good testimony with outsiders means a man's character must be visible and verified not only inside the warm circle of the church but out in the cold light of the marketplace, where reputations are not flattered. God screens His shepherds by who they are when no one is applauding.

es_reference.prompt: 24. ¿Por qué advierte la unidad contra ordenar a un nuevo convertido y exige buena reputación con los de afuera?
es_reference.model: La advertencia contra ordenar a un nuevo convertido (1 Timoteo 3:6) nombra no la incompetencia sino el orgullo — no sea que, envaneciéndose, caiga en la misma condenación del diablo. El requisito de buen testimonio con los de afuera significa que el carácter de un hombre debe ser visible y verificado no solo dentro del círculo cálido de la iglesia, sino fuera, en la luz fría del mercado, donde las reputaciones no se adulan. Dios examina a sus pastores por quiénes son cuando nadie aplaude.

sa.prompt: 25. Explain “Take heed to yourself and to the doctrine” and the image of the dry cistern.
sa.model: Paul's charge to Timothy puts the order beyond dispute: take heed to yourself first, and then to the doctrine. The man who reverses it—pouring all his care into his teaching while his own heart goes untended—is building a fine house on a rotting foundation. You cannot give your people water from a cistern you have let run dry. Every public word should be drawn from a private well the pastor is daily refilling in secret, alone with God.

es_reference.prompt: 25. Explique «Ten cuidado de ti mismo y de la doctrina» y la imagen de la cisterna seca.
es_reference.model: El encargo de Pablo a Timoteo pone el orden fuera de disputa: ten cuidado de ti mismo primero, y luego de la doctrina. El hombre que lo invierte — vertiendo todo su cuidado en su enseñanza mientras su propio corazón queda sin atender — edifica una hermosa casa sobre un cimiento podrido. Usted no puede dar a su gente agua de una cisterna que ha dejado secar. Cada palabra pública debe sacarse de un pozo privado que el pastor llena a diario en secreto, a solas con Dios.

sa.prompt: 26. Why are the spiritual disciplines called the “supply lines” of ministry rather than optional refinements?
sa.model: The spiritual disciplines are not optional refinements for the unusually devout pastor; they are the very supply lines of the ministry. They include prayer that is more than the hurried blessing before a meal, and the Word read for his own soul and not merely mined for next Sunday's sermon—for a man can study the Scriptures professionally for years and starve spiritually the whole time, like a baker who never eats the bread. The visible man in the pulpit must be matched by an invisible man on his knees, or the public man becomes a hollow performance.

es_reference.prompt: 26. ¿Por qué se llaman las disciplinas espirituales las «líneas de abastecimiento» del ministerio y no refinamientos opcionales?
es_reference.model: Las disciplinas espirituales no son refinamientos opcionales para el pastor inusualmente devoto; son las líneas mismas de abastecimiento del ministerio. Incluyen oración que sea más que la bendición apresurada antes de una comida, y la Palabra leída para su propia alma y no meramente explotada para el sermón del próximo domingo — pues un hombre puede estudiar las Escrituras profesionalmente por años y morir de hambre espiritualmente todo ese tiempo, como un panadero que nunca come el pan. El hombre visible en el púlpito debe corresponderse con un hombre invisible de rodillas, o el hombre público se vuelve una actuación hueca.

sa.prompt: 27. Why is pride the besetting sin of those who handle holy things, and what guards against it?
sa.model: Pride is the peculiar and besetting sin of those who handle holy things, because the very platform that makes a man useful makes him a target; the higher he is lifted in others' eyes, the deeper the pit that opens beneath his vanity. Over all his labor must hang the guard of humility. The shepherd who forgets that he is first a sheep, equally dependent on the grace he proclaims, has already begun to fall, however long the fall takes to become visible. Keep low—the ground is safest there.

es_reference.prompt: 27. ¿Por qué es el orgullo el pecado acosador de quienes manejan cosas santas, y qué lo guarda?
es_reference.model: El orgullo es el pecado peculiar y acosador de quienes manejan cosas santas, porque la misma plataforma que hace útil a un hombre lo hace blanco; cuanto más alto es levantado a los ojos de otros, más profundo el foso que se abre bajo su vanidad. Sobre toda su labor debe pender la guarda de la humildad. El pastor que olvida que es primero una oveja, igualmente dependiente de la gracia que proclama, ya ha comenzado a caer, por mucho que tarde la caída en hacerse visible. Manténgase bajo — el suelo es más seguro allí.

sa.prompt: 28. Explain how moral catastrophe is a slow drift rather than a sudden leap.
sa.model: Moral catastrophe is almost never a sudden leap. It is a slow drift—a series of small, deniable compromises, each one excused, that quietly carve a channel down which the final disaster will one day rush. The unguarded glance becomes the entertained thought; the entertained thought becomes the secret habit; the secret habit becomes the public scandal that ends a ministry. No man wakes up one morning and decides to destroy his life's work; he drifts there, one unconfessed inch at a time.

es_reference.prompt: 28. Explique cómo la catástrofe moral es una deriva lenta y no un salto repentino.
es_reference.model: La catástrofe moral casi nunca es un salto repentino. Es una deriva lenta — una serie de pequeñas concesiones negables, cada una excusada, que en silencio labran un canal por el cual un día se precipitará el desastre final. La mirada sin guardia se vuelve el pensamiento entretenido; el pensamiento entretenido se vuelve el hábito secreto; el hábito secreto se vuelve el escándalo público que termina un ministerio. Ningún hombre despierta una mañana y decide destruir la obra de su vida; llega allí a la deriva, una pulgada no confesada a la vez.

sa.prompt: 29. Why did even Paul discipline himself, and who is in the gravest danger?
sa.model: Even the apostle Paul refused to presume on his own standing: ‘I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, lest, when I have preached to others, I myself should become disqualified’ (1 Corinthians 9:27). If a man of Paul's stature guarded himself against his own ruin, then the man who thinks he has no need to guard himself is the man already in gravest danger. Confidence in one's own immunity is itself the first symptom of the fall.

es_reference.prompt: 29. ¿Por qué se disciplinó aun Pablo, y quién está en el más grave peligro?
es_reference.model: Aun el apóstol Pablo rehusó presumir de su propia posición: «sujeto mi cuerpo y lo pongo en servidumbre, no sea que habiendo predicado a otros, yo mismo venga a ser reprobado» (1 Corintios 9:27). Si un hombre de la estatura de Pablo se guardaba contra su propia ruina, entonces el hombre que cree no tener necesidad de guardarse es el que ya está en el más grave peligro. La confianza en la propia inmunidad es ella misma el primer síntoma de la caída.

sa.prompt: 30. List the safeguards against disqualification and the goal they aim at.
sa.model: The safeguards are honest accountability to men permitted to ask the hard questions and not be flattered out of asking them; a vigilant guard over the eyes, the schedule, and the private hours where ruin is seeded; a refusal to minister from isolation, since the lone shepherd is easiest to pick off; and the immediate confession of sin while it is still small, before it takes root in the dark. Guarding one's marriage belongs to this vigilance as well. The whole aim is the testimony every faithful minister longs to give at the end—‘I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith’—for the goal is not merely to begin well but to finish.

es_reference.prompt: 30. Enumere las salvaguardas contra la descalificación y la meta a la que apuntan.
es_reference.model: Las salvaguardas son rendir cuentas honestas a hombres a quienes se permite hacer las preguntas difíciles y que no se dejarán adular para no hacerlas; una guarda vigilante sobre los ojos, el horario y las horas privadas donde la ruina se siembra; una negativa a ministrar desde el aislamiento, pues el pastor solitario es el más fácil de derribar; y la confesión inmediata del pecado mientras aún es pequeño, antes de que eche raíces en la oscuridad. Guardar el matrimonio pertenece también a esta vigilancia. Toda la meta es el testimonio que todo ministro fiel anhela dar al final — «He peleado la buena batalla, he acabado la carrera, he guardado la fe» — pues la meta no es meramente comenzar bien sino terminar.
